coronary-artery-disease.name: Coronary artery disease
coronary-artery-disease.definition: Narrowing of the coronary arteries by fatty plaque (atherosclerosis), limiting blood flow to the heart muscle.
coronary-artery-disease.overview: Plaque builds up over decades in the arteries that supply the heart. When a narrowing limits flow during exertion the muscle becomes short of oxygen and signals this as angina; when a plaque ruptures and a clot blocks the artery, the result is a heart attack. It is the leading cause of death worldwide, and largely preventable.

structures: Trunk of anterior interventricular branch of left coronary artery
Circumflex branch of left coronary artery
Marginal branch of right coronary artery

causes: Atherosclerosis: cholesterol-rich plaque forming in the artery wall, driven by inflammation
riskFactors: Family history of early heart disease
signs: Often none between attacks
Signs of risk factors: high blood pressure, xanthelasma, nicotine staining
coronary-artery-disease.diagnosis: The story of exertional chest pressure relieved by rest is the key. An ECG may be normal at rest; a stress test, CT coronary angiography or invasive angiography shows the narrowings. Blood tests assess cholesterol, glucose and kidney function.
coronary-artery-disease.treatment: Lifestyle change and medication for everyone: stop smoking, statins to lower LDL, aspirin to prevent clots, blood pressure and diabetes control, and drugs to relieve angina (nitrates, beta blockers). Significant narrowings can be opened with angioplasty and a stent or bypassed with surgery.
coronary-artery-disease.prevention: Not smoking, regular exercise, a diet low in saturated fat and salt, healthy weight, and treating blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes.
coronary-artery-disease.seekCare: Call emergency services for chest pain lasting more than a few minutes, or angina that is new, more frequent or occurs at rest.

myocardial-infarction.name: Heart attack (myocardial infarction)
myocardial-infarction.definition: Death of heart muscle because a coronary artery is suddenly blocked, usually by a clot forming on a ruptured plaque.
myocardial-infarction.overview: Every minute of blockage kills more muscle, so a heart attack is treated as a race to reopen the artery. Survival and the amount of muscle saved depend on how quickly the person calls for help and reaches a hospital able to perform emergency angioplasty.

structures: Trunk of anterior interventricular branch of left coronary artery
Posterior interventricular branch of right coronary artery

causes: Rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque with clot formation
Less often: coronary spasm, spontaneous artery dissection, severe anaemia or oxygen lack with a fixed narrowing
riskFactors: Same as coronary artery disease: smoking, cholesterol, blood pressure, diabetes, family history, age
signs: Pale, sweaty, distressed
Fast or slow pulse, low or high blood pressure
Crackles in the lungs if the heart is failing
complications: Rupture of the heart wall or a papillary muscle
myocardial-infarction.diagnosis: An ECG within ten minutes of arrival shows ST elevation (STEMI) when a large artery is fully blocked; troponin in the blood rises over hours and confirms muscle damage in other cases. Echocardiography shows which wall has stopped moving.
myocardial-infarction.treatment: Aspirin immediately, then emergency angioplasty with a stent to reopen the artery (or clot-dissolving drugs if angioplasty is not reachable within about two hours). Afterwards: a second antiplatelet drug, a statin, a beta blocker and an ACE inhibitor, cardiac rehabilitation and risk factor control.
myocardial-infarction.prevention: The measures that prevent coronary artery disease; after a first attack, lifelong medication and rehabilitation halve the risk of another.
myocardial-infarction.seekCare: Call emergency services immediately for crushing chest pain, pain spreading to the arm or jaw, or chest discomfort with sweating, breathlessness or nausea. Do not drive yourself.

heart-failure.name: Heart failure
heart-failure.definition: A syndrome in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs, or can do so only at raised filling pressures.
heart-failure.overview: Heart failure is the end result of damage from heart attacks, high blood pressure, valve disease or cardiomyopathy. Blood backs up behind the failing ventricle: fluid in the lungs causes breathlessness, fluid in the tissues causes swelling. It is a chronic condition managed with drugs that reduce the heart's workload and, in some cases, devices.
causes: Coronary artery disease and previous heart attacks
High blood pressure
Valve disease
Cardiomyopathies (genetic, viral, alcohol, chemotherapy)
Atrial fibrillation
Congenital heart disease
signs: Raised jugular venous pressure
Crackles at the lung bases
Pitting ankle oedema
Enlarged liver
Third heart sound
heart-failure.diagnosis: Blood natriuretic peptide (BNP) is raised; echocardiography measures the ejection fraction and finds the cause. ECG, chest X-ray and blood tests for kidney function and anaemia complete the picture.
heart-failure.treatment: Diuretics relieve fluid overload; ACE inhibitors or ARNI, beta blockers, mineralocorticoid antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors prolong life in reduced ejection fraction. Salt and fluid moderation, daily weights, vaccination and exercise rehabilitation. Selected patients receive pacemakers, defibrillators or, rarely, transplantation.
heart-failure.prevention: Treating blood pressure and coronary disease early, limiting alcohol, and controlling diabetes.
heart-failure.seekCare: Seek urgent help for breathlessness at rest, waking at night gasping, pink frothy sputum, chest pain, fainting, or rapid weight gain (more than 2 kg in three days).

atrial-fibrillation.name: Atrial fibrillation
atrial-fibrillation.definition: A common heart rhythm disorder in which the atria quiver chaotically instead of contracting, producing an irregular and often fast pulse.
atrial-fibrillation.overview: In atrial fibrillation the sinoatrial node loses control and hundreds of electrical impulses a minute swirl through the atria; the atrioventricular node lets an irregular selection through. Blood stagnates in the fibrillating left atrium and can clot, which is why AF causes one in five strokes.
causes: High blood pressure
Coronary artery disease and heart failure
Valve disease, especially mitral
Overactive thyroid
Alcohol binges
Lung disease and sleep apnoea
Often no single cause in older people
signs: Irregularly irregular pulse
Pulse deficit (heart rate higher than the wrist pulse)
complications: Heart failure from a persistently fast rate
atrial-fibrillation.diagnosis: An ECG shows no P waves and an irregular rhythm. Brief episodes are caught with a Holter or patch monitor or a wearable. Echocardiography looks for valve disease and atrial size; blood tests check thyroid function.
atrial-fibrillation.treatment: Two decisions: control the rate (beta blockers, calcium-channel blockers, digoxin) or restore rhythm (cardioversion, antiarrhythmic drugs, catheter ablation), and prevent stroke with an anticoagulant when the risk score justifies it. Treat the underlying causes.
atrial-fibrillation.prevention: Control blood pressure, weight, alcohol and sleep apnoea; keep active.
atrial-fibrillation.seekCare: Urgent care for palpitations with chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness, and emergency services for any stroke symptoms.

hypertension.name: High blood pressure (hypertension)
hypertension.definition: Persistently raised arterial pressure, usually defined as 140/90 mmHg or more in the clinic (135/85 on home readings).
hypertension.overview: High blood pressure rarely causes symptoms but silently damages arteries, heart, brain, kidneys and eyes over years. It affects around one adult in three and is the single biggest contributor to stroke and heart disease worldwide. Treatment is cheap and effective, yet half of those affected do not know they have it.
causes: Primary (essential) hypertension in over 90%: genes, salt, weight, alcohol, inactivity, age
Secondary causes in the rest: kidney disease, adrenal tumours, narrowed renal arteries, sleep apnoea, some drugs (NSAIDs, steroids, the pill), pregnancy
signs: Usually none; very high pressure can show retinal changes, an enlarged heart or kidney damage
hypertension.diagnosis: Repeated readings in clinic confirmed by home or 24-hour ambulatory monitoring. Blood and urine tests, an ECG and eye examination look for organ damage and secondary causes.
hypertension.treatment: Lifestyle first: less salt, weight loss, exercise, less alcohol. Drugs when readings stay high or risk is raised: ACE inhibitors or ARBs, calcium-channel blockers, thiazide-like diuretics, added stepwise; most people need two or more.
hypertension.prevention: A diet rich in fruit, vegetables and low in salt, regular activity, healthy weight, moderate alcohol and no smoking.
hypertension.seekCare: A reading above 180/120 with headache, chest pain, breathlessness, vision change or confusion is a hypertensive emergency.

deep-vein-thrombosis.name: Deep vein thrombosis
deep-vein-thrombosis.definition: A blood clot in a deep vein, most often of the calf or thigh.
deep-vein-thrombosis.overview: Clots form when blood flow slows, the vein wall is injured or the blood clots too easily (Virchow's triad). A leg DVT causes pain and swelling; its danger is that a fragment can break off and lodge in the lungs as a pulmonary embolism.
causes: Immobility: surgery, long flights, bed rest, plaster casts
Cancer and chemotherapy
Pregnancy, the combined pill and hormone replacement
Inherited clotting tendencies (factor V Leiden and others)
Injury to the vein
signs: One calf swollen more than 3 cm larger than the other, warm, tender, with dilated surface veins
complications: Post-thrombotic syndrome: chronic swelling, pain and skin ulcers
deep-vein-thrombosis.diagnosis: A clinical probability score, a D-dimer blood test to rule out low-risk cases, and compression ultrasound of the leg veins to confirm.
deep-vein-thrombosis.treatment: Anticoagulation for at least three months, usually with a direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, rivaroxaban) or warfarin; compression stockings for symptoms; early mobilisation. Large clots occasionally need catheter-directed clot removal.
deep-vein-thrombosis.prevention: Move early after surgery, use prescribed stockings and injections in hospital, walk and hydrate on long journeys, stop smoking.
deep-vein-thrombosis.seekCare: Same-day assessment for a swollen painful calf; emergency care if breathlessness or chest pain develops.

pulmonary-embolism.name: Pulmonary embolism
pulmonary-embolism.definition: Blockage of a pulmonary artery by a clot that has travelled from a vein, usually in the leg or pelvis.
pulmonary-embolism.overview: A pulmonary embolism cuts off blood flow to part of the lung: the affected segment is ventilated but not perfused, oxygen levels fall and the right ventricle strains against the obstruction. Small emboli cause pleuritic pain and breathlessness; a large one can cause collapse and death within minutes.
causes: Deep vein thrombosis of the leg or pelvis
Rarely fat, air or amniotic fluid emboli
signs: Fast breathing and pulse
Low oxygen saturation
Signs of DVT in a leg
Low blood pressure in massive PE
pulmonary-embolism.diagnosis: Probability scoring and D-dimer, then CT pulmonary angiography to show the clot; ventilation-perfusion scanning in pregnancy or kidney disease. ECG and echocardiography assess strain on the right heart.
pulmonary-embolism.treatment: Immediate anticoagulation (low-molecular-weight heparin, then a direct oral anticoagulant or warfarin for three to six months or longer); clot-dissolving drugs or catheter removal for massive PE with shock; oxygen and support.
pulmonary-embolism.prevention: DVT prevention: early mobilisation, prophylactic injections in hospital, compression stockings, keeping moving on long journeys.
pulmonary-embolism.seekCare: Emergency services for sudden breathlessness, chest pain on breathing, coughing blood or collapse, especially with a swollen leg or recent surgery.

stroke.name: Stroke
stroke.definition: Sudden loss of brain function because blood supply to part of the brain is interrupted, by a blocked artery (ischaemic, 85%) or a bleed (haemorrhagic).
stroke.overview: Brain tissue dies within minutes of losing its blood supply, and the lost functions map the artery: weakness and numbness of the opposite side, loss of speech, loss of half the visual field, or unsteadiness and double vision from the brainstem. Treatment to reopen the artery works only in the first hours, so stroke is a medical emergency recognised by the FAST test.
causes: Atherosclerosis of the carotid and cerebral arteries
Emboli from the heart in atrial fibrillation
Small vessel disease from high blood pressure and diabetes
Bleeding from high blood pressure, aneurysms or vascular malformations
Arterial dissection in younger people
signs: Facial droop
Arm drift
Slurred or absent speech
Loss of a visual field
Unsteady gait
stroke.diagnosis: Immediate CT to distinguish a bleed from a blockage, then CT or MR angiography to find the blocked vessel. Blood glucose is checked at once to exclude hypoglycaemia. ECG, echocardiography and carotid ultrasound search for the source.
stroke.treatment: For ischaemic stroke, clot-dissolving thrombolysis within 4.5 hours and mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel blockage within 6 to 24 hours, then antiplatelet drugs, statins, blood pressure control and anticoagulation if AF is found. Bleeds need blood pressure control, reversal of anticoagulants and sometimes surgery. Rehabilitation by a stroke team drives recovery.
stroke.prevention: Treat blood pressure and atrial fibrillation, stop smoking, control diabetes and cholesterol, exercise, and manage weight and alcohol.
stroke.seekCare: Call emergency services immediately at any sign of Face drooping, Arm weakness or Speech difficulty: Time matters. Symptoms that resolve (a TIA) still need same-day assessment.

migraine.name: Migraine
migraine.definition: A recurrent headache disorder with attacks of moderate to severe throbbing pain, typically one-sided, lasting 4 to 72 hours, with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound.
migraine.overview: Migraine is a disorder of brain excitability rather than of blood vessels alone. A wave of altered activity spreading across the cortex explains the aura that a third of sufferers experience, and activation of the trigeminal pain pathway explains the headache. It affects about one person in seven and is the leading cause of disability in young women.
causes: Inherited susceptibility with triggers: sleep change, missed meals, stress and stress release, hormones, alcohol, certain foods, bright light, weather
signs: Normal examination between and usually during attacks
complications: Chronic migraine (15 or more headache days a month)
Slightly raised stroke risk in migraine with aura, especially with smoking and the combined pill
migraine.diagnosis: Clinical, from the pattern of attacks; a headache diary helps. Scans are needed only for red-flag features such as a change in pattern, abnormal examination or a thunderclap onset.
migraine.treatment: Attacks: a triptan taken early, plus an NSAID or paracetamol and an anti-sickness drug; rest in a dark room. Prevention when attacks are frequent: propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate, candesartan, CGRP antibody injections, and avoiding identified triggers.
migraine.prevention: Regular sleep and meals, hydration, limiting caffeine and alcohol, exercise, stress management, and limiting painkillers to fewer than 10 days a month.
migraine.seekCare: Emergency care for a headache that is the worst ever or peaks within a minute, or comes with fever, stiff neck, weakness, confusion or a first-ever aura after 50.

epilepsy.name: Epilepsy
epilepsy.definition: A tendency to recurrent, unprovoked seizures: bursts of abnormal synchronised electrical activity in the brain.
epilepsy.overview: Seizures take many forms depending on where they start: a focal seizure may cause twitching of one hand, an odd smell or a period of unresponsive staring; a generalised tonic-clonic seizure involves loss of consciousness, stiffening and jerking of the whole body. Most people with epilepsy become seizure-free on medication.
causes: Often unknown or genetic
Scarring from stroke, head injury, infection or birth injury
Brain tumours and malformations
Hippocampal sclerosis
Dementia in older people
signs: Usually normal between seizures
Post-seizure confusion, bitten tongue, incontinence
complications: Status epilepticus (a seizure over five minutes: an emergency)
epilepsy.diagnosis: A witness account or video is the most useful evidence. An EEG may show epileptic discharges; MRI looks for a structural cause; blood tests exclude metabolic causes and an ECG excludes a cardiac cause of collapse.
epilepsy.treatment: Anti-seizure medication chosen by seizure type (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, valproate and others), taken consistently. Surgery, laser ablation or nerve stimulation for drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Seizure first aid education for family.
epilepsy.prevention: Take medication regularly, sleep well, limit alcohol, avoid known triggers; helmets and safe driving reduce head injuries that cause acquired epilepsy.
epilepsy.seekCare: Call emergency services for a seizure lasting more than five minutes, repeated seizures without recovery, a first seizure, injury, or difficulty breathing afterwards.

parkinsons-disease.name: Parkinson's disease
parkinsons-disease.definition: A progressive disorder in which dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra of the midbrain are lost, causing slowness, stiffness and tremor.
parkinsons-disease.overview: The basal ganglia need dopamine to release intended movements smoothly. As nigral neurons die, movements become slow and small, muscles stiff, and a resting tremor appears, typically starting on one side. Non-motor features such as loss of smell, constipation, sleep disturbance and later cognitive change are part of the disease.
causes: Accumulation of misfolded alpha-synuclein protein in neurons; the trigger is unknown in most cases
Genetic forms in a minority
Rare toxin exposure
signs: Resting tremor (pill-rolling)
Bradykinesia: slow, small movements
Rigidity (cogwheeling)
Stooped posture, shuffling gait, reduced arm swing
Reduced facial expression, soft voice, small handwriting
parkinsons-disease.diagnosis: Clinical, by a neurologist, on the combination of bradykinesia with tremor or rigidity and a response to levodopa. MRI excludes other causes; a DaT scan can confirm dopamine loss when uncertain.
parkinsons-disease.treatment: Levodopa remains the most effective drug; dopamine agonists, MAO-B and COMT inhibitors extend its effect. Physiotherapy, exercise, speech and occupational therapy maintain function. Deep brain stimulation helps selected patients with fluctuations.
parkinsons-disease.prevention: No proven prevention; regular exercise and coffee are linked to lower risk and exercise slows decline.
parkinsons-disease.seekCare: See a doctor for a new tremor at rest, slowing of movement or a change in gait; urgent help for falls with injury, inability to swallow, or sudden confusion.

alzheimers-disease.name: Alzheimer's disease
alzheimers-disease.definition: The commonest cause of dementia: a progressive loss of memory and thinking ability caused by the build-up of amyloid plaques and tau tangles and the death of neurons, beginning in the hippocampus.
alzheimers-disease.overview: Alzheimer's starts years before symptoms, with abnormal proteins accumulating in the medial temporal lobes. Early disease affects the formation of new memories; over years it spreads to language, spatial skills, judgement and finally basic bodily functions. It affects one person in ten over 65 and one in three over 85.
causes: Accumulation of amyloid-beta and tau proteins with loss of synapses and neurons
Rare inherited forms with early onset
riskFactors: Cardiovascular risk factors: hypertension, diabetes, smoking, obesity
Low education, hearing loss, social isolation, depression, inactivity
signs: Poor recall of recent events with preserved distant memory
Word-finding difficulty
Getting lost in familiar places
Impaired judgement and planning
Later: personality change, incontinence, immobility
complications: Infections, especially pneumonia and urinary infections
alzheimers-disease.diagnosis: History from the person and a relative, cognitive testing, blood tests to exclude thyroid, B12 and other reversible causes, and MRI showing hippocampal shrinkage. Amyloid PET or spinal fluid markers can confirm the diagnosis in specialist settings.
alzheimers-disease.treatment: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil) and memantine give modest symptomatic benefit; anti-amyloid antibodies can slow early disease in selected patients. Structured routines, cognitive stimulation, treating hearing loss and depression, carer support and advance care planning matter as much.
alzheimers-disease.prevention: Up to 40% of dementia is attributable to modifiable factors: control blood pressure, stay physically, socially and mentally active, treat hearing loss, do not smoke, limit alcohol.
alzheimers-disease.seekCare: Forgetting recent conversations, repeating questions, getting lost or struggling with familiar tasks over months should prompt a memory assessment; sudden confusion over hours or days is delirium and needs urgent review.

asthma.name: Asthma
asthma.definition: A chronic inflammatory disease of the airways causing reversible narrowing, with episodes of wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness and cough.
asthma.overview: In asthma the bronchial lining is chronically inflamed and over-reactive. Triggers such as allergens, viruses, exercise or cold air make the smooth muscle constrict and the lining swell and pour out mucus. Between attacks breathing may be normal. It affects about one child in ten and one adult in twelve.
causes: Genetic susceptibility plus environmental exposure: allergens (dust mite, pollen, pets), early viral infections, tobacco smoke, air pollution, occupational chemicals
riskFactors: Family history of asthma or allergy
signs: Widespread wheeze on breathing out
Fast breathing, use of accessory muscles in an attack
A silent chest and exhaustion in a life-threatening attack
complications: Side effects of repeated steroid courses
asthma.diagnosis: Variable symptoms plus evidence of variable airflow obstruction: spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility, peak-flow variability, or raised exhaled nitric oxide and blood eosinophils.
asthma.treatment: Inhaled corticosteroids are the foundation, combined with a long-acting bronchodilator as needed; a reliever inhaler for symptoms; a written action plan; trigger avoidance; biologic injections for severe allergic or eosinophilic asthma. Attacks are treated with high-dose reliever, oral steroids and oxygen.
asthma.prevention: Avoid smoking and smoke exposure, control allergens, have flu vaccination, use the preventer inhaler daily and check inhaler technique.
asthma.seekCare: Emergency care if the reliever is not helping, the person cannot speak in sentences, lips are blue, or peak flow is below a third of best.

copd.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
copd.definition: Progressive, largely irreversible airflow obstruction caused by damage to the airways (chronic bronchitis) and destruction of alveoli (emphysema), almost always from smoking.
copd.overview: Years of inhaled smoke inflame the small airways and dissolve the alveolar walls, so air is trapped and the surface for gas exchange shrinks. Breathlessness on exertion creeps up over decades and is often blamed on age; flare-ups triggered by infections drive hospital admissions. COPD is the third leading cause of death worldwide.
causes: Tobacco smoking (85 to 90% of cases)
Biomass and cooking-fire smoke
Occupational dust and fumes
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (inherited)
riskFactors: Childhood respiratory infections and poor lung growth
signs: Barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing
Wheeze and reduced breath sounds
Cyanosis and ankle oedema in advanced disease
complications: Pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure (cor pulmonale)
copd.diagnosis: Spirometry showing an FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7 that does not fully reverse with a bronchodilator, in someone with symptoms and a smoking or exposure history. Chest X-ray and CT exclude other causes and grade emphysema.
copd.treatment: Stopping smoking is the only measure that slows decline. Long-acting bronchodilator inhalers (with inhaled steroids for frequent exacerbators), pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccinations, and oxygen at home for low oxygen levels. Exacerbations are treated with steroids and often antibiotics.
copd.prevention: Never smoking, or stopping at any stage; clean cooking fuels; workplace dust control; vaccination against flu, pneumococcus and COVID-19.
copd.seekCare: Urgent review for worsening breathlessness with more or discoloured sputum, fever, or confusion and drowsiness (a sign of carbon dioxide retention).

pneumonia.name: Pneumonia
pneumonia.definition: Infection of the alveoli, which fill with fluid and inflammatory cells so that part of the lung cannot exchange gas.
pneumonia.overview: Bacteria (most often Streptococcus pneumoniae), viruses (influenza, COVID-19, RSV) and occasionally fungi cause pneumonia. It ranges from a mild illness treated at home to a life-threatening one in the elderly, the very young and those with chronic disease, and it remains the leading infectious cause of death in children worldwide.
causes: Bacteria: pneumococcus, Haemophilus, Mycoplasma, Legionella, Staphylococcus
Viruses: influenza, SARS-CoV-2, RSV
Aspiration of stomach contents
Hospital-acquired organisms in ventilated or frail patients
riskFactors: Weak immune system, diabetes, heart, kidney or liver disease
signs: Fast breathing, fever, crackles and dull percussion over the affected lobe
Low oxygen saturation
Confusion in the elderly
pneumonia.diagnosis: Clinical findings plus a chest X-ray showing consolidation. Blood tests (white cells, CRP, kidney function), oxygen saturation, sputum and blood cultures, and a severity score (CURB-65) guide where and how to treat.
pneumonia.treatment: Antibiotics chosen by likely organism and severity (amoxicillin for mild community-acquired pneumonia; combinations in hospital), antivirals for influenza, oxygen, fluids, and support of breathing in severe cases. Rest and hydration at home for mild cases.
pneumonia.prevention: Pneumococcal, influenza and COVID-19 vaccination, stopping smoking, good hand hygiene, and managing chronic diseases.
pneumonia.seekCare: Urgent care for breathlessness at rest, confusion, blue lips, chest pain, coughing blood, or fever with fast breathing in a child or older adult.

lung-cancer.name: Lung cancer
lung-cancer.definition: A malignant tumour arising from the lining of the airways or alveoli, divided into non-small-cell (about 85%) and small-cell types.
lung-cancer.overview: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death because it is usually found late: symptoms appear only when a tumour blocks an airway, invades the chest wall or spreads. Smoking causes about eight in ten cases. Low-dose CT screening of heavy smokers finds tumours early enough to cure.
causes: Tobacco smoke
Radon gas
Asbestos, diesel exhaust and other occupational carcinogens
Air pollution
Family history
signs: Finger clubbing
Hoarse voice
Enlarged lymph nodes in the neck
Signs of a pleural effusion or collapsed lobe
Weight loss
complications: Spread to lymph nodes, liver, bones, brain and adrenals
lung-cancer.diagnosis: Chest X-ray then CT of the chest and abdomen; tissue by bronchoscopy or CT-guided biopsy; PET-CT for staging; molecular tests on the tumour to guide targeted therapy.
lung-cancer.treatment: Depends on type and stage: surgery or radical radiotherapy for early non-small-cell cancer; chemotherapy, immunotherapy and targeted drugs (for EGFR, ALK and other mutations) for advanced disease; chemotherapy and radiotherapy for small-cell cancer; palliative care for symptoms throughout.
lung-cancer.prevention: Not smoking is the single most effective measure; radon testing of homes; workplace protection; CT screening for eligible heavy smokers.
lung-cancer.seekCare: See a doctor within days for a cough lasting three weeks, coughing blood, unexplained breathlessness, weight loss or a new hoarse voice, especially if you smoke or have smoked.

appendicitis.name: Appendicitis
appendicitis.definition: Acute inflammation of the appendix, usually because its opening into the caecum is blocked.
appendicitis.overview: The appendix is a blind pouch hanging off the caecum in the lower right abdomen. When its lumen is obstructed, by a hard pellet of stool, swollen lymphoid tissue or rarely a tumour, bacteria multiply, pressure rises, the wall becomes inflamed and, within a day or two, can perforate. It is the commonest cause of emergency abdominal surgery.
causes: Obstruction of the appendix lumen by a faecolith or enlarged lymphoid tissue
Rarely a tumour or parasite
signs: Tenderness and guarding at McBurney's point in the right lower quadrant
Rebound tenderness
Pain on the right when the left side is pressed (Rovsing's sign)
Mild fever and fast pulse
appendicitis.diagnosis: Largely clinical: the migrating pain, tenderness and raised white cells and CRP. Ultrasound in children and pregnancy; CT in adults when the picture is unclear. A pregnancy test in women excludes an ectopic pregnancy.
appendicitis.treatment: Prompt removal of the appendix (appendectomy), now usually laparoscopic, with antibiotics before and, if perforated, after surgery. Selected uncomplicated cases can be treated with antibiotics alone, with a risk of recurrence. An abscess may be drained first and the appendix removed later.
appendicitis.seekCare: Same-day emergency assessment for pain that moves to the lower right abdomen, worsens over hours, and comes with nausea, loss of appetite or fever.

gerd.name: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease
gerd.definition: Reflux of stomach acid into the oesophagus often enough to cause symptoms or damage the lining.
gerd.overview: The lower oesophageal sphincter normally keeps acid in the stomach. When it relaxes too often or is weakened, especially with a hiatus hernia or obesity, acid burns the unprotected oesophagus. Heartburn after meals and lying down is the classic symptom; chronic reflux can scar the oesophagus or change its lining (Barrett's oesophagus), a precursor of cancer.
causes: Weak or over-relaxing lower oesophageal sphincter
Hiatus hernia
Raised abdominal pressure: obesity, pregnancy
Delayed stomach emptying
riskFactors: Alcohol, coffee, fatty and spicy food, large late meals
Some drugs: NSAIDs, calcium-channel blockers, nitrates
signs: Usually none
Dental erosion, hoarseness
gerd.diagnosis: Typical symptoms responding to acid suppression are usually enough. Endoscopy is done for alarm features (difficulty swallowing, weight loss, bleeding, anaemia, onset over 55) or persistent symptoms; pH monitoring quantifies reflux when the diagnosis is unclear.
gerd.treatment: Weight loss, smaller earlier meals, raising the bed head, avoiding triggers, stopping smoking. Antacids and alginates for occasional symptoms; proton pump inhibitors for regular symptoms and healing. Anti-reflux surgery (fundoplication) for severe cases.
gerd.prevention: Healthy weight, not smoking, moderate alcohol and coffee, no large meals within three hours of bed.
gerd.seekCare: See a doctor promptly for difficulty or pain swallowing, vomiting blood, black stools, unexplained weight loss, or heartburn that persists despite treatment; chest pain that could be cardiac needs emergency assessment.

peptic-ulcer.name: Peptic ulcer
peptic-ulcer.definition: A break in the lining of the stomach or duodenum that extends through the mucosa, caused by acid acting on a weakened defence.
peptic-ulcer.overview: Most peptic ulcers are caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori or by NSAID painkillers, both of which strip the mucus barrier that protects the lining from acid. Duodenal ulcers are commoner and classically hurt when hungry; gastric ulcers hurt after eating. Ulcers can bleed or perforate.
causes: Helicobacter pylori infection
NSAIDs and aspirin
Rarely: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, severe physiological stress, Crohn's disease
riskFactors: Steroids and anticoagulants taken with NSAIDs
signs: Epigastric tenderness
Signs of anaemia if bleeding chronically
Rigid abdomen if perforated
complications: Bleeding: vomiting blood or passing black stools
peptic-ulcer.diagnosis: Testing for H. pylori (breath, stool or blood test); endoscopy to see the ulcer, take biopsies and treat bleeding, especially in those over 55 or with alarm features.
peptic-ulcer.treatment: Eradicate H. pylori with a proton pump inhibitor plus two antibiotics for one to two weeks; stop NSAIDs; proton pump inhibitor for four to eight weeks to heal. Bleeding ulcers are treated endoscopically; perforation needs surgery.
peptic-ulcer.prevention: Avoid NSAIDs when possible or take a protective proton pump inhibitor with them, stop smoking, limit alcohol.
peptic-ulcer.seekCare: Emergency care for vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, black tarry stools, sudden severe abdominal pain, or collapse.

gallstones.name: Gallstones
gallstones.definition: Hard deposits, usually of cholesterol, that form in the gallbladder when bile becomes supersaturated.
gallstones.overview: Gallstones are present in about one adult in ten and most cause no trouble. Symptoms begin when a stone blocks the gallbladder outlet (biliary colic), inflames the gallbladder (cholecystitis), or escapes into the bile duct where it causes jaundice, infection of the bile (cholangitis) or pancreatitis.
causes: Cholesterol supersaturation of bile with sluggish gallbladder emptying
Pigment stones from red cell breakdown (haemolysis) or infection
signs: Right upper quadrant tenderness worse on breathing in (Murphy's sign)
Fever in cholecystitis
Jaundice with a duct stone
gallstones.diagnosis: Ultrasound shows stones and a thickened gallbladder wall; liver function tests and lipase detect duct obstruction and pancreatitis; MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound finds duct stones.
gallstones.treatment: Silent stones need no treatment. Symptomatic stones: laparoscopic removal of the gallbladder (cholecystectomy), ideally within days of a cholecystitis attack; duct stones are removed endoscopically (ERCP). Pain relief, fluids and antibiotics for infection.
gallstones.prevention: Healthy weight lost gradually, regular meals, a diet high in fibre and low in refined carbohydrate.
gallstones.seekCare: Urgent assessment for abdominal pain lasting more than a few hours, pain with fever or shivering, or yellowing of the skin or eyes.

inflammatory-bowel-disease.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
inflammatory-bowel-disease.definition: Chronic inflammation of the gut driven by an abnormal immune response: ulcerative colitis affects the colon's lining continuously from the rectum; Crohn's disease can affect any part of the tract, in patches and through the full wall thickness.
inflammatory-bowel-disease.overview: IBD typically begins in the teens and twenties and follows a relapsing course. Ulcerative colitis brings bloody diarrhoea and urgency; Crohn's brings pain, diarrhoea, weight loss, mouth ulcers and complications such as strictures and fistulas. Modern immune-modulating drugs control most cases, but surgery is still needed by many.
causes: Interaction of genes, the gut microbiome and an over-active mucosal immune response
Over 200 susceptibility genes identified
riskFactors: Smoking (for Crohn's; it is protective in ulcerative colitis)
NSAIDs and antibiotics may trigger flares
signs: Weight loss, anaemia
Abdominal tenderness or a mass
Perianal fistulas and skin tags in Crohn's
Mouth ulcers, eye inflammation, joint swelling
inflammatory-bowel-disease.diagnosis: Blood tests (anaemia, CRP), faecal calprotectin to distinguish from irritable bowel, stool cultures to exclude infection, colonoscopy with biopsies, and MRI of the small bowel for Crohn's.
inflammatory-bowel-disease.treatment: Aminosalicylates for mild ulcerative colitis; steroids to settle flares; thiopurines, methotrexate and biologic antibodies (anti-TNF, anti-integrin, anti-IL-23) or JAK inhibitors to maintain remission; nutritional therapy in Crohn's; surgery for complications or refractory colitis.
inflammatory-bowel-disease.prevention: No known prevention; not smoking reduces Crohn's flares and complications.
inflammatory-bowel-disease.seekCare: Urgent care for more than six bloody stools a day with fever or a fast pulse, severe abdominal pain and distension, or inability to keep fluids down.

colorectal-cancer.name: Colorectal (bowel) cancer
colorectal-cancer.definition: A malignant tumour of the colon or rectum, almost always arising from a benign polyp (adenoma) over years.
colorectal-cancer.overview: Bowel cancer is the third commonest cancer worldwide. Because it grows slowly from polyps, screening by stool testing and colonoscopy can find and remove growths before they turn malignant. Early cancers are cured by surgery; symptoms usually appear late, so screening participation matters.
causes: Accumulated genetic mutations in the lining cells, usually sporadic
Inherited syndromes: Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis
riskFactors: Processed and red meat, low fibre, obesity, inactivity
signs: Change in bowel habit lasting weeks
Blood in or on the stool
Iron-deficiency anaemia
A palpable mass
Weight loss
complications: Spread to liver, lungs and peritoneum
colorectal-cancer.diagnosis: Faecal immunochemical test for screening or triage, then colonoscopy with biopsy; CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging; MRI of the rectum; blood CEA marker.
colorectal-cancer.treatment: Surgery to remove the tumour and lymph nodes is the mainstay; chemotherapy after surgery for higher-risk disease; radiotherapy and chemotherapy before surgery for rectal cancer; chemotherapy, targeted and immune drugs for spread; liver metastases are sometimes resectable.
colorectal-cancer.prevention: Take part in screening from the age offered, eat fibre and less processed meat, keep active and a healthy weight, do not smoke, limit alcohol; aspirin lowers risk in Lynch syndrome.
colorectal-cancer.seekCare: See a doctor within days for blood in the stool, a change in bowel habit lasting three weeks, unexplained weight loss or anaemia; emergency care for severe pain with vomiting and a swollen abdomen.

cirrhosis.name: Cirrhosis
cirrhosis.definition: Scarring of the liver from long-term damage, in which nodules of regenerating cells are surrounded by fibrous bands that distort blood flow and impair function.
cirrhosis.overview: Years of injury from alcohol, fatty liver disease or viral hepatitis replace liver tissue with scar. The result is failure of the liver's jobs (jaundice, bleeding, confusion) and high pressure in the portal vein (varices, fluid in the abdomen, an enlarged spleen). Cirrhosis is irreversible, but stopping the cause halts progression.
causes: Alcohol
Metabolic dysfunction-associated (fatty) liver disease
Hepatitis B and C
Autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis
Haemochromatosis, Wilson's disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
riskFactors: Unprotected sex or injected drug use (viral hepatitis)
signs: Jaundice, spider naevi, red palms
Enlarged spleen, ascites
Muscle wasting, bruising
Confusion and a flapping tremor (encephalopathy)
cirrhosis.diagnosis: Liver function tests, clotting and platelet count; ultrasound or elastography (FibroScan) measuring stiffness; tests for the cause (hepatitis viruses, iron, autoantibodies); endoscopy for varices; six-monthly ultrasound for cancer surveillance.
cirrhosis.treatment: Remove the cause: complete abstinence from alcohol, weight loss, antivirals for hepatitis B and C. Diuretics for ascites, beta blockers or banding for varices, lactulose for encephalopathy, nutrition, vaccination. Liver transplantation for decompensated disease.
cirrhosis.prevention: Drink within recommended limits or not at all, keep a healthy weight, vaccinate against hepatitis B, never share needles, treat hepatitis C.
cirrhosis.seekCare: Emergency care for vomiting blood, black stools, confusion or drowsiness, a rapidly swelling abdomen with fever, or deepening jaundice.

pancreatitis.name: Pancreatitis
pancreatitis.definition: Inflammation of the pancreas, acute when its own enzymes are activated inside the gland, chronic when repeated injury leads to scarring and loss of function.
pancreatitis.overview: Gallstones and alcohol cause four in five cases of acute pancreatitis. Activated enzymes digest the gland and surrounding fat, and severe cases trigger a body-wide inflammatory response with organ failure. Most attacks are mild and settle in days; chronic pancreatitis causes lasting pain, malabsorption and diabetes.
causes: Gallstones blocking the duct
Alcohol
High triglycerides, high calcium
Some drugs (azathioprine, valproate, thiazides)
After ERCP
Viral infections, trauma, genetic mutations
signs: Severe epigastric tenderness
Fast pulse, low blood pressure in severe disease
Bruising of the flanks or around the navel in haemorrhagic cases
Jaundice with a duct stone
complications: Organ failure and death in severe attacks
Diabetes and malabsorption in chronic disease
Pancreatic cancer risk in chronic pancreatitis
pancreatitis.diagnosis: Typical pain with a serum lipase or amylase more than three times normal; ultrasound for gallstones; CT after 48 to 72 hours if severe to assess necrosis; blood tests to score severity.
pancreatitis.treatment: Intravenous fluids, pain relief, early feeding when tolerated; ERCP to remove a duct stone with cholangitis; antibiotics and drainage for infected necrosis; cholecystectomy before discharge for gallstone pancreatitis. Chronic disease: stop alcohol and smoking, enzyme supplements, pain management, diabetes care.
pancreatitis.prevention: Moderate alcohol, treat gallstones once symptomatic, control triglycerides, stop smoking.
pancreatitis.seekCare: Emergency care for severe constant upper abdominal pain radiating to the back with vomiting, especially after alcohol or with known gallstones.

osteoarthritis.name: Osteoarthritis
osteoarthritis.definition: The commonest joint disease: progressive loss of articular cartilage with changes in the underlying bone, causing pain and stiffness, most often in the knees, hips, hands and spine.
osteoarthritis.overview: Osteoarthritis is not simply wear: it is a failed repair process in which cartilage thins, bone thickens and forms spurs (osteophytes), and the joint lining becomes intermittently inflamed. Pain builds over years, worse with use and at the end of the day. It affects most people over 65 to some degree.
causes: Mechanical load on a susceptible joint: age, previous injury, malalignment, obesity
Genetic factors, especially in hand OA
riskFactors: Heavy manual work or elite sport
signs: Bony enlargement, crepitus, reduced range of motion
Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes on the fingers
Effusion in a flared knee
Antalgic gait
osteoarthritis.diagnosis: Clinical in a person over 45 with activity-related pain and brief morning stiffness. X-rays show joint-space narrowing, sclerosis and osteophytes but correlate poorly with symptoms; blood tests are normal and are used to exclude inflammatory arthritis.
osteoarthritis.treatment: Exercise and strengthening, weight loss, education and pacing are the core treatments. Topical NSAIDs, paracetamol and oral NSAIDs for pain; walking aids and braces; steroid injections for flares. Joint replacement when pain limits life despite these.
osteoarthritis.prevention: Healthy weight, regular low-impact exercise, strong muscles around the joints, and avoiding joint injury.
osteoarthritis.seekCare: See a doctor for joint pain limiting daily activities; urgent care for a hot, red, swollen joint with fever.

rheumatoid-arthritis.name: Rheumatoid arthritis
rheumatoid-arthritis.definition: A chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the synovial lining of joints, causing symmetrical inflammation that can destroy cartilage and bone.
rheumatoid-arthritis.overview: Rheumatoid arthritis typically starts in the small joints of the hands and feet with prolonged morning stiffness and swelling, and can involve the eyes, lungs, heart and blood vessels. Untreated it deforms and disables; started early, disease-modifying drugs now prevent most damage.

structures: Proximal phalanx of right index finger

causes: Autoimmunity against citrullinated proteins, in genetically susceptible people, often triggered by smoking or infection
signs: Symmetrical swelling of metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints
Morning stiffness over an hour
Rheumatoid nodules
Later: ulnar deviation, swan-neck deformities
rheumatoid-arthritis.diagnosis: Clinical pattern plus rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies, raised CRP and ESR, and ultrasound or X-ray showing synovitis and erosions. Early referral to rheumatology within weeks changes outcomes.
rheumatoid-arthritis.treatment: Methotrexate started early, with short-term steroids to control symptoms; biologic drugs (anti-TNF, anti-IL-6, B-cell depletion) or JAK inhibitors if disease stays active; NSAIDs for pain; physiotherapy, occupational therapy and cardiovascular risk management.
rheumatoid-arthritis.prevention: Not smoking and good dental health reduce risk; early treatment prevents damage.
rheumatoid-arthritis.seekCare: See a doctor within weeks for swelling of several joints with morning stiffness; urgent care for a single hot joint with fever or new neck pain with tingling in the arms.

osteoporosis.name: Osteoporosis
osteoporosis.definition: Loss of bone mass and deterioration of bone architecture that makes bones fragile and prone to fracture after minimal trauma.
osteoporosis.overview: Bone is constantly remodelled; after the peak mass reached around 30, resorption slowly outpaces formation, sharply so in women after the menopause. Osteoporosis is silent until a bone breaks: the wrist, spine or hip. Hip fractures in older adults carry a high risk of death and loss of independence, and are largely preventable.
causes: Oestrogen loss at the menopause
Ageing
Long-term steroid treatment
Low calcium and vitamin D, malabsorption
Overactive thyroid or parathyroid, low testosterone
Immobility
riskFactors: Female sex, early menopause, or long gaps in sex-hormone exposure (including after removal of the ovaries or testes)
signs: Loss of height, stooped posture (kyphosis)
Fragility fracture after a fall from standing height
osteoporosis.diagnosis: DXA bone density scan (a T-score of −2.5 or lower), fracture risk calculators (FRAX), spine X-ray for vertebral fractures, and blood tests for vitamin D, calcium, thyroid and other secondary causes.
osteoporosis.treatment: Calcium and vitamin D sufficiency, weight-bearing and balance exercise, fall prevention; bisphosphonates (alendronate) first line, denosumab or teriparatide for severe disease; treat secondary causes.
osteoporosis.prevention: Build peak bone mass with exercise and calcium in youth, keep active, do not smoke, limit alcohol, ensure vitamin D, review medicines that cause falls or bone loss.
osteoporosis.seekCare: Any fracture from a minor fall after 50, sudden back pain in an older person, or loss of more than 4 cm in height should prompt assessment.

fracture.name: Bone fracture
fracture.definition: A break in the continuity of a bone, from a hairline crack to a shattered, displaced or open injury.
fracture.overview: Bones break when the force exceeds their strength: a fall on the outstretched hand fractures the wrist, a twist the ankle, a car crash the femur. In weakened bone (osteoporosis, cancer) a minor force is enough. Bone heals by forming a callus that is remodelled over months; the aim of treatment is to hold the fragments in a good position while it does.
causes: Trauma: falls, sport, road accidents, assaults
Repeated stress (stress fractures in runners and soldiers)
Weakened bone: osteoporosis, tumours, infection
riskFactors: Poor balance, medicines that cause falls
signs: Pain, swelling, bruising, deformity
Inability to bear weight or use the limb
Crepitus
Open wound over the bone in open fractures
fracture.diagnosis: X-rays in two views; CT for complex joint, spine and pelvic fractures; MRI for occult fractures such as the scaphoid or stress fractures; assessment of circulation and nerves beyond the break.
fracture.treatment: Realign (reduce) if displaced, then hold: a cast or splint for stable fractures, or surgery with plates, screws, nails or external fixation for unstable ones. Pain relief, elevation, early movement of neighbouring joints, and physiotherapy. Open fractures need urgent cleaning and antibiotics.
fracture.prevention: Fall prevention and bone health in older adults, protective equipment in sport, road safety, treating osteoporosis.
fracture.seekCare: Emergency care for deformity, a bone through the skin, numbness or a cold pale limb, or a suspected hip, spine or pelvic fracture; same-day care for any inability to bear weight or use a limb after injury.

acl-injury.name: Anterior cruciate ligament injury
acl-injury.definition: A sprain or tear of the anterior cruciate ligament, the band inside the knee that stops the tibia sliding forward on the femur and controls rotation.
acl-injury.overview: ACL tears happen in a moment: a pivot, a sudden stop or a landing with the knee twisted inward, often with a pop and rapid swelling. The knee then gives way on turning. Young athletes, especially women, are most affected. Whether to reconstruct the ligament depends on the person's activity and instability.

structures: Long head of right biceps femoris

causes: Non-contact pivoting, cutting or landing injuries (70%)
Direct blows to the knee
riskFactors: Poor landing mechanics and hip weakness
signs: A pop at injury, swelling within hours (haemarthrosis)
Positive Lachman and anterior drawer tests
Giving way on pivoting
acl-injury.diagnosis: History and examination; MRI confirms the tear and shows associated meniscal, collateral ligament and bone injuries. X-rays exclude fracture.
acl-injury.treatment: Immediate: rest, ice, compression, elevation and early physiotherapy. Structured rehabilitation restores function in many people; surgical reconstruction with a tendon graft (hamstring, patellar or quadriceps) is chosen for those with instability or pivoting sports, followed by 9 to 12 months of rehabilitation.
acl-injury.prevention: Neuromuscular training programmes (landing technique, hip and hamstring strength, balance) cut injury rates by half in athletes.
acl-injury.seekCare: Same-day assessment for a knee that swelled rapidly after a twisting injury, cannot straighten, locks or feels unstable.

disc-herniation.name: Herniated (slipped) disc
disc-herniation.definition: Protrusion of the soft nucleus of an intervertebral disc through its fibrous outer ring, most often at the lower lumbar levels, which can press on a nerve root.
disc-herniation.overview: Discs weaken with age and can bulge or rupture under load. Most herniations cause back pain alone; when the extruded material compresses a nerve root the result is sciatica: sharp pain, tingling and numbness shooting down the leg in that root's territory, sometimes with weakness. Nine in ten settle within three months without surgery.

structures: Intervertebral disk of fourth lumbar vertebra
Intervertebral disk of fifth lumbar vertebra
Intervertebral disk of fifth cervical vertebra

causes: Age-related disc degeneration
Lifting, twisting or a sudden strain
Repetitive loading
signs: Pain reproduced by straight-leg raising
Reduced ankle or knee reflex
Weak ankle dorsiflexion or big toe extension
Sensory loss in a dermatome
disc-herniation.diagnosis: Clinical, with MRI reserved for red flags, progressive neurological deficit or when surgery or injection is being considered, because disc bulges are common in people without symptoms.
disc-herniation.treatment: Stay active, pain relief (NSAIDs, short courses of stronger analgesia), physiotherapy, and time. Epidural steroid injections for severe radicular pain. Microdiscectomy for persistent sciatica beyond six to twelve weeks or for progressive weakness; emergency decompression for cauda equina syndrome.
disc-herniation.prevention: Lift with the legs, keep the back and core strong, healthy weight, do not smoke.
disc-herniation.seekCare: Emergency care for numbness around the saddle area, difficulty passing urine or controlling bowels, or weakness in both legs; urgent review for progressive weakness or unbearable pain.

gout.name: Gout
gout.definition: An inflammatory arthritis caused by deposition of uric acid crystals in joints, triggered when blood urate is persistently high.
gout.overview: Uric acid is a waste product of purine metabolism. When its level exceeds saturation it crystallises in cool joints, classically the big toe, and the crystals provoke a sudden, exquisitely painful attack. Repeated attacks damage joints and form lumps (tophi). Lowering urate with medication dissolves the crystals and prevents attacks.

structures: Proximal phalanx of right big toe

causes: Reduced kidney excretion of urate (90%)
Overproduction: high purine diet, cell breakdown, rare enzyme defects
riskFactors: Alcohol (beer and spirits), sugary drinks, red meat and shellfish
signs: A red, hot, shiny, extremely tender joint, often the first metatarsophalangeal joint
Tophi on the ears, fingers and elbows in chronic gout
complications: Association with heart disease and kidney disease
gout.diagnosis: Crystals seen in joint fluid confirm it; a raised serum urate supports it (but may be normal during an attack); ultrasound or dual-energy CT shows crystal deposits. Infection must be excluded in a single hot joint.
gout.treatment: Attacks: NSAIDs, colchicine or steroids, started early; rest and ice. Prevention: allopurinol (or febuxostat) started after the attack settles and titrated to a target urate, with cover against flares for the first months; weight loss and diet changes.
gout.prevention: Healthy weight, limit alcohol and sugary drinks, moderate red meat and seafood, stay hydrated, review diuretics.
gout.seekCare: Same-day assessment for a hot swollen joint with fever, since septic arthritis looks identical and is an emergency.

type-1-diabetes.name: Type 1 diabetes
type-1-diabetes.definition: An autoimmune disease in which the insulin-producing beta cells of the pancreas are destroyed, so the body cannot regulate blood glucose without injected insulin.
type-1-diabetes.overview: Type 1 diabetes usually appears in childhood or young adulthood over days to weeks: thirst, frequent urination, weight loss and tiredness as glucose spills into the urine. Without insulin the body burns fat uncontrollably and produces acid (ketoacidosis), which is fatal untreated. Lifelong insulin replacement, increasingly with pumps and continuous glucose monitors, allows a full life.
causes: Autoimmune destruction of beta cells in genetically susceptible people, possibly triggered by viral infection
signs: Weight loss, dehydration
Ketone smell, deep sighing breathing and drowsiness in ketoacidosis
type-1-diabetes.diagnosis: Raised blood glucose with symptoms; ketones in blood or urine; antibodies (GAD, IA-2) and low C-peptide confirm type 1. HbA1c tracks control over months.
type-1-diabetes.treatment: Insulin from diagnosis, as multiple daily injections (long-acting plus rapid-acting with meals) or a pump, matched to carbohydrate intake; glucose monitoring; structured education; annual screening of eyes, kidneys and feet; blood pressure and cholesterol control.
type-1-diabetes.prevention: None yet, although immunotherapy can delay onset in high-risk relatives; good control prevents complications.
type-1-diabetes.seekCare: Emergency care for vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing, drowsiness or confusion in someone with diabetes, or for severe hypoglycaemia (confusion, seizure, unconsciousness).

type-2-diabetes.name: Type 2 diabetes
type-2-diabetes.definition: A metabolic disease in which the body's cells respond poorly to insulin (insulin resistance) and the pancreas gradually fails to compensate, leaving blood glucose persistently high.
type-2-diabetes.overview: Type 2 diabetes accounts for over 90% of diabetes and is closely tied to excess weight and inactivity, though genes matter greatly. It develops silently over years; many people are diagnosed on a routine test or when a complication appears. Sustained weight loss early on can put it into remission.
causes: Insulin resistance from visceral fat and inactivity, plus progressive beta-cell failure, on a strong genetic background
riskFactors: Age over 40 (younger in South Asian, Black and Hispanic populations)
signs: Often none
Central obesity, acanthosis nigricans
Reduced foot sensation and pulses in established disease
Retinal changes
type-2-diabetes.diagnosis: HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or more, or fasting glucose of 7 mmol/L or more, repeated if without symptoms. Annual checks of kidney function, urine albumin, eyes, feet, blood pressure and lipids.
type-2-diabetes.treatment: Diet, weight loss and activity are the foundation; metformin first, then SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists, DPP-4 inhibitors, sulfonylureas or insulin as needed; statins and blood pressure treatment reduce cardiovascular risk; structured education and foot care.
type-2-diabetes.prevention: Diet and exercise programmes halve the risk in people with prediabetes; keeping a healthy weight and staying active are the key measures.
type-2-diabetes.seekCare: Urgent care for very high glucose readings with drowsiness or confusion, a foot wound that is red, hot or discharging, sudden vision change, or chest pain.

hypothyroidism.name: Underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism)
hypothyroidism.definition: Insufficient thyroid hormone, most often because the immune system destroys the thyroid gland, slowing the body's metabolism.
hypothyroidism.overview: Thyroxine sets the pace of nearly every cell, so its lack slows everything: energy, thought, bowel, heart rate and heat production. Symptoms creep in over months and are easily mistaken for ageing or depression. A simple blood test makes the diagnosis and a daily tablet of levothyroxine restores normal life.
causes: Autoimmune (Hashimoto's) thyroiditis
Treatment of an overactive thyroid (radioiodine, surgery)
Iodine deficiency worldwide
Drugs: amiodarone, lithium, immunotherapy
Pituitary failure (rare)
Congenital
signs: Weight gain, dry skin and hair, puffy face
Slow pulse, cold intolerance
Slow-relaxing reflexes
Goitre
Hoarse voice, constipation, heavy periods
hypothyroidism.diagnosis: A raised TSH with a low free T4 confirms primary hypothyroidism; thyroid peroxidase antibodies indicate the autoimmune cause. Cholesterol is often raised.
hypothyroidism.treatment: Levothyroxine once daily on an empty stomach, dose adjusted by TSH every six to eight weeks until stable, then checked yearly; higher doses are needed in pregnancy.
hypothyroidism.prevention: Adequate iodine intake; screening in pregnancy and after thyroid treatment.
hypothyroidism.seekCare: See a doctor for persistent tiredness with weight gain, cold intolerance or low mood; emergency care for drowsiness, very low temperature or confusion in someone with known hypothyroidism.

hyperthyroidism.name: Overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism)
hyperthyroidism.definition: Excess thyroid hormone, most often from Graves' disease, in which antibodies stimulate the thyroid to overproduce.
hyperthyroidism.overview: Too much thyroxine speeds the body up: weight loss despite appetite, tremor, palpitations, sweating, anxiety and diarrhoea. Graves' disease can also inflame the eye muscles, pushing the eyes forward. Treatment blocks hormone production, destroys thyroid tissue with radioiodine, or removes the gland.
causes: Graves' disease (autoimmune, 75%)
Toxic multinodular goitre and toxic adenoma
Thyroiditis releasing stored hormone
Excess thyroxine tablets, amiodarone, iodine loads
signs: Fast pulse, atrial fibrillation, tremor, warm moist skin
Goitre, sometimes with a bruit
Eye signs: lid retraction, protrusion, double vision
Weight loss, brisk reflexes
complications: Thyroid eye disease with vision loss
hyperthyroidism.diagnosis: Suppressed TSH with raised free T4 or T3; TSH-receptor antibodies confirm Graves'; a radioiodine uptake scan distinguishes causes when antibodies are negative.
hyperthyroidism.treatment: Beta blockers for symptoms; antithyroid drugs (carbimazole, propylthiouracil) for 12 to 18 months; radioiodine or thyroidectomy for relapse or large goitres, followed by levothyroxine replacement. Eye disease needs specialist care and stopping smoking.
hyperthyroidism.prevention: Not smoking reduces eye disease; no prevention for the autoimmune process itself.
hyperthyroidism.seekCare: Urgent care for palpitations with breathlessness or chest pain, fever with confusion and agitation, or sudden vision change or eye pain.

urinary-tract-infection.name: Urinary tract infection
urinary-tract-infection.definition: Bacterial infection of the bladder (cystitis) or, when it ascends, the kidney (pyelonephritis), usually by gut bacteria such as Escherichia coli.
urinary-tract-infection.overview: UTIs are among the commonest bacterial infections, far more frequent in women because the short urethra lets bacteria reach the bladder easily. Cystitis burns and nags but is rarely dangerous; kidney infection causes fever, loin pain and vomiting and can lead to sepsis, especially in the elderly, in pregnancy and with obstruction.
causes: Gut bacteria (E. coli in 80%) ascending the urethra
Catheters and instrumentation
Obstruction: stones, enlarged prostate
riskFactors: Female anatomy (a short urethra close to the vagina and anus), sexual activity, spermicides
Incomplete bladder emptying, kidney stones, prostate enlargement
signs: Suprapubic tenderness
Loin tenderness and fever in pyelonephritis
Confusion in older adults
Cloudy or bloody urine
urinary-tract-infection.diagnosis: Symptoms and a urine dipstick (nitrites, leucocytes, blood) in uncomplicated cystitis; urine culture in men, children, pregnancy, recurrent or complicated infection; blood tests and imaging if kidney infection or obstruction is suspected.
urinary-tract-infection.treatment: A short course of antibiotics (nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim for cystitis; longer courses of a broader agent for kidney infection), fluids and pain relief. Intravenous antibiotics for severe infection; relief of any obstruction.
urinary-tract-infection.prevention: Fluids, emptying the bladder after sex, avoiding spermicides, vaginal oestrogen after the menopause, prophylactic antibiotics or methenamine for frequent recurrences.
urinary-tract-infection.seekCare: Urgent care for fever, shivering, loin pain, vomiting or confusion with urinary symptoms, symptoms in pregnancy or in a man, or blood in the urine that persists.

kidney-stones.name: Kidney stones
kidney-stones.definition: Hard crystals, most commonly calcium oxalate, that form in the kidney and can pass into and block the ureter.
kidney-stones.overview: Stones form when urine is concentrated and rich in stone-forming salts. A stone leaving the kidney scrapes and blocks the ureter, producing renal colic: waves of agonising pain from the loin to the groin with blood in the urine. Most stones under 5 mm pass on their own; larger or infected obstructions need intervention.
causes: Low urine volume
High urinary calcium, oxalate or uric acid
Urinary infection with urease-producing bacteria (struvite stones)
Rare inherited causes (cystinuria)
riskFactors: High salt, animal protein and oxalate intake
signs: Restless, unable to lie still
Loin tenderness
Blood in the urine on dipstick
Fever if infected
complications: Recurrence in half within ten years
kidney-stones.diagnosis: Non-contrast CT of the urinary tract is the definitive test; ultrasound in pregnancy and children; urine dipstick and culture, kidney function and calcium and urate levels; analysis of the passed stone.
kidney-stones.treatment: Strong analgesia (NSAIDs are most effective), fluids, and drugs to relax the ureter to help small stones pass; shock-wave lithotripsy, ureteroscopy with laser fragmentation or percutaneous surgery for larger stones; urgent drainage with a stent or nephrostomy if obstructed and infected.
kidney-stones.prevention: Drink enough to pass 2 to 2.5 litres of urine a day, limit salt and animal protein, keep normal calcium intake, lemon juice for citrate; specific drugs for recurrent formers.
kidney-stones.seekCare: Emergency care for colicky pain with fever or shivering, vomiting preventing fluids, pain not controlled by painkillers, or a single functioning kidney.

chronic-kidney-disease.name: Chronic kidney disease
chronic-kidney-disease.definition: Persistent reduction in kidney function (a filtration rate below 60 ml/min) or evidence of kidney damage such as protein in the urine, for more than three months.
chronic-kidney-disease.overview: The kidneys lose nephrons slowly and silently, most often from diabetes and high blood pressure. Symptoms appear only when function is severely reduced, so CKD is found by blood and urine tests in at-risk people. Progression can be slowed for years; a minority reach kidney failure needing dialysis or transplantation.
causes: Diabetes
High blood pressure
Glomerulonephritis
Polycystic kidney disease
Obstruction (prostate, stones)
Recurrent infection, drugs (NSAIDs, lithium), reflux
riskFactors: Black, South Asian and Indigenous ancestry
signs: High blood pressure
Oedema
Pallor from anaemia
Late: itching, muscle twitching, drowsiness
complications: Cardiovascular disease (the leading cause of death in CKD)
chronic-kidney-disease.diagnosis: Estimated GFR from blood creatinine and the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, repeated over three months; ultrasound of the kidneys; tests for the cause. CKD is staged G1 to G5 and A1 to A3.
chronic-kidney-disease.treatment: Blood pressure control with ACE inhibitors or ARBs, SGLT2 inhibitors, statins, glucose control, salt restriction, stopping smoking, avoiding NSAIDs, dose adjustment of medicines; treating anaemia and bone disease; preparing for dialysis or transplantation as function declines.
chronic-kidney-disease.prevention: Control diabetes and blood pressure, keep a healthy weight, do not smoke, avoid regular NSAIDs, stay hydrated during illness, have kidney checks if at risk.
chronic-kidney-disease.seekCare: Urgent care for breathlessness, chest pain, severe drowsiness, or a sudden fall in urine output; routine review for swelling, frothy urine or persistently high blood pressure.

anaemia.name: Anaemia
anaemia.definition: A haemoglobin concentration below normal (roughly under 130 g/L in men and 120 g/L in women), reducing the blood's capacity to carry oxygen.
anaemia.overview: Anaemia is a sign, not a diagnosis. Iron deficiency from blood loss or poor intake is the commonest cause worldwide; others include vitamin B12 and folate deficiency, chronic disease, kidney failure, inherited haemoglobin disorders and bone marrow failure. Finding the cause matters because in adults it can be bleeding from a bowel cancer.
causes: Iron deficiency: heavy periods, gut bleeding, poor diet, malabsorption, pregnancy
Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency
Chronic inflammation or kidney disease
Thalassaemia and sickle cell disease
Haemolysis
Bone marrow disease
signs: Pale conjunctivae and palms
Fast pulse, flow murmur
Spoon nails, sore tongue in iron deficiency
Jaundice in haemolysis
Numb feet and unsteadiness in B12 deficiency
anaemia.diagnosis: Full blood count with red cell size (MCV) points to the type; ferritin, B12, folate, reticulocytes and a blood film narrow it down; coeliac tests and endoscopy or colonoscopy find gut causes of iron deficiency in men and older women.
anaemia.treatment: Treat the cause; oral iron for three months after correction (or intravenous iron if not tolerated), B12 injections or folate, erythropoietin in kidney disease, transfusion only for severe or symptomatic anaemia.
anaemia.prevention: Iron-rich diet with vitamin C, treating heavy periods, iron supplements in pregnancy where advised, avoiding unnecessary NSAIDs.
anaemia.seekCare: Urgent care for breathlessness at rest, chest pain, fainting, or black or bloody stools; routine review for persistent tiredness and pallor.

sepsis.name: Sepsis
sepsis.definition: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated body response to infection.
sepsis.overview: Any infection can trigger sepsis, most often pneumonia, urinary infection, abdominal infection or skin infection. The immune response spills over into the whole body: blood vessels leak and dilate, clotting is disturbed, and organs fail. Sepsis kills millions a year; each hour of delay in antibiotics raises mortality, so recognition is everything.
causes: Bacterial infection most often (pneumococcus, E. coli, staphylococci, streptococci, meningococcus)
Viral, fungal or parasitic infections
riskFactors: Weak immune system: chemotherapy, steroids, diabetes, no spleen
Pregnancy and the weeks after birth
signs: Fast breathing (over 22/min), fast pulse, low blood pressure
New confusion or drowsiness
Mottled, cold or clammy skin; non-blanching rash
Passing little urine
Very high or abnormally low temperature
complications: Acute kidney injury, lung failure, liver failure
sepsis.diagnosis: Clinical recognition (NEWS or qSOFA scores), blood cultures and cultures from the likely source before antibiotics, lactate, blood counts, kidney and liver function, clotting; imaging to find the source.
sepsis.treatment: The 'sepsis six' within an hour: oxygen, blood cultures, intravenous antibiotics, intravenous fluids, lactate measurement and urine output monitoring; then source control (drain an abscess, remove an infected line), vasopressors and organ support in intensive care.
sepsis.prevention: Vaccination, hand hygiene, prompt treatment of infections, careful care of wounds and catheters, and knowing the warning signs.
sepsis.seekCare: Call emergency services for an infection with slurred speech or confusion, extreme shivering or muscle pain, passing no urine in a day, severe breathlessness, mottled or discoloured skin, or a feeling of impending doom; for children also fast breathing, a fit, blue or pale skin, a non-fading rash, or unusual drowsiness.

breast-cancer.name: Breast cancer
breast-cancer.definition: A malignant tumour arising from the cells that line the ducts or lobules of the breast. It may remain within the ducts (in situ) or invade the surrounding tissue and spread to the axillary lymph nodes and beyond.
breast-cancer.overview: Breast cancer is the commonest cancer in women worldwide, and most cases occur after 50. Most tumours start in the milk ducts, fewer in the milk-producing lobules; ductal carcinoma in situ stays within the duct, while invasive cancer has broken through it. Every invasive cancer is tested for oestrogen receptors, progesterone receptors and the HER2 protein, which with grade and stage decides treatment. It is rare in men, and anyone with breast tissue can develop it.

structures: Sternocostal part of left pectoralis major
Sternocostal part of right pectoralis major

causes: Accumulated DNA damage in duct or lobule cells, driven in part by lifetime exposure to oestrogen and progesterone
Inherited faults in BRCA1, BRCA2 and a few other genes, responsible for a minority of cases
Previous radiotherapy to the chest, particularly in youth
No single cause is found in most cases; ageing is the strongest factor
riskFactors: Increasing age: most cases are diagnosed after 50
A close relative with breast or ovarian cancer, or a known BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation
Longer lifetime oestrogen exposure: an early first period, a late menopause, no pregnancies or a first pregnancy late in life
Combined hormone replacement therapy and, to a small degree, the combined contraceptive pill: the increase is small, relates to how long they are used, and falls after stopping
Alcohol, and being overweight after the menopause
Dense breast tissue on mammography, a previous breast cancer or some benign breast conditions

In trans women, several years of feminising hormone therapy: the risk is thought to be higher than in cis men but lower than in cis women; in men, conditions that raise oestrogen levels such as obesity, Klinefelter syndrome and cirrhosis
signs: A firm, irregular, usually painless lump in the breast or armpit
Dimpling, puckering or an orange-peel texture of the skin over the breast
A newly inverted nipple, a rash or crusting on the nipple, or blood-stained discharge
A change in the size or outline of one breast
In advanced disease, bone pain, breathlessness or jaundice from spread to bone, lung or liver
complications: Spread to the axillary lymph nodes and to bone, lung, liver or brain (metastatic breast cancer)
Lymphoedema of the arm after axillary surgery or radiotherapy
Bone loss and menopausal symptoms from endocrine therapy; heart effects of some chemotherapy and HER2-targeted drugs
Recurrence in the breast, chest wall or elsewhere, sometimes many years later
Anxiety, altered body image and loss of fertility in younger patients
breast-cancer.diagnosis: A suspicious lump or nipple change is assessed in a one-stop breast clinic by triple assessment: clinical examination, imaging (mammography, with ultrasound for younger women and dense breasts) and a core needle biopsy of anything abnormal. The biopsy confirms invasive or in situ disease, grade and receptor status (oestrogen receptor, progesterone receptor and HER2). Ultrasound of the axilla with needle sampling of suspicious nodes, and MRI in selected cases, complete local staging; CT and bone scans are reserved for larger tumours, involved nodes or symptoms suggesting spread. Genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 is offered when the age at diagnosis, tumour type or family history suggests an inherited cause. Screening in England invites women, and anyone else registered female with a GP who has breast tissue, for mammography every three years; the first invitation arrives between the ages of 50 and 53, routine invitations stop after 70, and anyone aged 71 or over can still ask their local breast screening service for screening. Trans women who have taken hormones for some years and trans men who have not had chest surgery may need to ask to be included.
breast-cancer.treatment: Early breast cancer is treated with surgery: either wide local excision, removing the tumour with a margin of normal tissue and followed by radiotherapy to the rest of the breast, or mastectomy, in each case with sentinel lymph node biopsy to check the axilla and clearance of the nodes if they are involved. Reconstruction can be immediate or delayed. Treatment given after surgery, or before it to shrink a large tumour, is chosen by receptor status and the risk of recurrence: chemotherapy; endocrine therapy for oestrogen-receptor-positive cancers (tamoxifen, or an aromatase inhibitor after the menopause), taken for years; and trastuzumab or similar antibodies for HER2-positive disease. Metastatic breast cancer is not usually curable but is often controlled for years with endocrine, targeted and chemotherapy, radiotherapy for painful bone deposits and bone-protecting drugs. Care is planned by a multidisciplinary team following NICE guidance.
breast-cancer.prevention: Not all breast cancer can be prevented, but keeping to a healthy weight, being physically active, limiting alcohol and breastfeeding all lower the risk, and hormone replacement therapy is best reviewed regularly and continued only for as long as it is needed. Attending screening finds cancers before they can be felt. People at high risk because of family history or a BRCA mutation can be offered earlier and more frequent imaging, risk-reducing medicines or risk-reducing surgery, planned with a genetics service.
breast-cancer.seekCare: See a GP promptly about any new lump in the breast or armpit, skin dimpling, a change in a nipple or blood-stained nipple discharge, in anyone with breast tissue, at any age and whatever their gender. Chest masculinisation removes most but not all of the breast tissue, so a new lump or change in the chest wall still needs the same assessment. NICE recommends urgent referral to a breast clinic for an unexplained breast lump in anyone aged 30 or over and for discharge, retraction or other changes of one nipple in anyone aged 50 or over. A hot, red, swollen breast with fever suggests infection and should be seen the same day; a red, inflamed breast that does not settle with antibiotics also needs referral.
